---
title: "Early Stopping"
description: "A training strategy that stops optimization when held-out performance stops improving."
term: "Early Stopping"
letter: "E"
category: "Model Training"
difficulty: "Beginner"
---

## Simple explanation

Early stopping ends model training when performance on a validation set
stops improving. It can help avoid spending time on updates that make the
model fit its training data more closely without improving generalization.

## Technical explanation

Training metrics and validation metrics are monitored at regular
intervals. A stopping rule tracks a chosen validation metric, often with
a patience period that allows small fluctuations. The model checkpoint
with the best validation result may be restored after stopping.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Training for too long can overfit and wastes compute. Early stopping is
a practical form of regularization and resource control, but depends on
a representative validation set and an appropriate metric.

## How it works

At each epoch or evaluation step, calculate the selected metric on
validation data. Save a checkpoint when it improves. Stop if it fails to
improve for the configured patience, and select the best checkpoint
rather than assuming the final one is best.

## Practical example

A vision model can be evaluated after every epoch. If validation loss
stops improving for several epochs while training loss keeps falling,
the training run can stop and restore the checkpoint with the lowest
validation loss.

## Common misconceptions

- Early stopping does not guarantee that the selected model generalizes
  to every deployment setting.
- Repeatedly tuning choices against the same validation set can overfit
  the model-selection process to that set.
- Stopping at the first small fluctuation can be premature; patience and
  metric noise should be considered.
